title: Prisoners and boxes
objectives: Use the cycle-following strategy and find its chance of success.

screens.title: Follow the numbers
screens.prose: Four prisoners, numbered 1 to 4, face four boxes holding their numbers in a random order. Each may open 2 boxes. Prisoner 1 opens box 1, then the box named by the number inside, and so on. Each arrow runs from a box to the box its number names.

state.caption: Box 1 holds 2, box 2 holds 4, box 3 holds 3, box 4 holds 1.

screens.question: Tap the boxes prisoner 1 opens, in order, until he finds number 1.

hints.text: He starts at his own box, box 1.
Box 1 holds 2, so he opens box 2 next.
Box 2 holds 4, and box 4 holds 1: boxes 1, 2, 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at box 1 and follow each arrow.

byKey.b3: Box 3 holds 3: it is a loop of its own, and prisoner 1 never reaches it.
byKey.order: Right boxes, wrong order. Follow the arrows from box 1.

explain.text: Box 1 sends him to box 2, box 2 to box 4, and box 4 holds his number 1. His chain is a cycle of length 3, so with 2 openings he fails. Prisoner 3 finds his number at once, in a cycle of length 1.

screens.title: Which orders win
screens.prose: Every prisoner follows the numbers from his own box. He succeeds exactly when his cycle has length at most 2. Opening 2 boxes at random instead, the team wins with chance $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$.

state.caption: All 24 orders of 4 numbers in 4 boxes, sorted by their cycles.

screens.question: With cycle-following, what is the team's chance of success?

hints.text: The team wins when every cycle has length 1 or 2.
Those rows hold 1, 6 and 3 orders.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the orders whose longest cycle is at most 2.

byKey.random: That is random opening. Following the numbers does much better.
byKey.half: That is one prisoner's chance, not the team's.
byKey.fourteen: You counted the losing orders: $8 + 6 = 14$. The team wins in the other 10.

explain.text: The team wins exactly when no cycle is longer than 2: $1 + 6 + 3 = 10$ of the 24 orders. So the chance is $10/24 = 5/12 \approx 0.4167$, against $0.0625$ at random. Principle: make everyone's success hang on one shared event.

screens.title: Six prisoners
screens.prose: Six prisoners each open 3 of 6 boxes, following the numbers. The team fails exactly when some cycle is longer than 3. A cycle of length $k$ appears with chance $1/k$ when $k > 3$, and two such cycles cannot fit in 6 boxes.

state.caption: The three ways to fail are separate events.

screens.question: What is the team's chance of success?

hints.text: Add the chances of failure.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the chance of a cycle longer than 3 from 1.

byKey.sum: That is the chance of failure. Subtract it from 1.
byKey.half: That is one prisoner's chance alone.

explain.text: Failure means one cycle of length 4, 5 or 6, and only one can occur. So the chances add: $1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6 = 37/60$. Success is $23/60 \approx 0.3833$, which a count of all 720 orders confirms.

screens.title: Each has a half
screens.prose: Now 100 prisoners each open 50 of 100 boxes. A candidate says each prisoner finds his number with chance $1/2$, so the team wins with chance $(1/2)^{100}$, essentially zero.
screens.question: Roughly what is the team's chance with cycle-following?

options.why: You multiplied the prisoners' chances as if independent. Under the strategy they succeed or fail together.
Half is one prisoner's chance. The team needs every cycle short.
69% is the chance of a cycle longer than 50, which is when the team fails.

hints.text: Does one prisoner's success tell you about another's?
Everyone in a long cycle fails together.
The team fails only when a cycle is longer than 50, about 69% of the time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The successes are linked by the cycles, not independent.

byKey.zero: Multiplying assumes independence. Cycle-following links every prisoner's fate to the longest cycle.
byKey.half: The team wins only if all cycles are short, which is less likely than one being short.
byKey.69: That is the failure chance. Success is about 31%.

explain.text: Each prisoner's chance is still $1/2$, but the events are not independent. Everyone succeeds exactly when no cycle exceeds 50, which happens about 31% of the time. Principle: a shared strategy can correlate outcomes.

screens.title: Counting long cycles
screens.prose: Take $k > n/2$. Count the orders of $n$ numbers in $n$ boxes that hold a cycle of length exactly $k$. Order the lines; two may swap and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the count.

lines.text: Choose the $k$ boxes on the cycle: $\binom{n}{k}$ ways.
Join them into one cycle: $(k - 1)!$ ways.
Arrange the other $n - k$ boxes freely: $(n - k)!$ ways.
Divide by the $n!$ orders: a $k$-cycle has chance $1/k$.
Join them into one cycle: $k!$ ways.
lines.why: A cycle has no first box, so its $k$ rotations are one cycle: $k!/k = (k - 1)!$.

hints.text: Choose, join, arrange the rest, then multiply.
A cycle of $k$ boxes can start anywhere.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cycle's boxes, the cycle, then the rest.

byKey.d1: Rotating a cycle gives the same cycle, so there are $(k - 1)!$, not $k!$.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the $k!$ line belongs.

explain.text: Choosing, joining and arranging give $\binom{n}{k}(k-1)!(n-k)! = n!/k$ orders. Since $k > n/2$, an order holds at most one such cycle, so nothing is counted twice. Dividing by $n!$ gives $1/k$.

screens.title: A hundred prisoners
screens.prose: Back to 100 prisoners opening 50 each. The team fails when a cycle has length $k$ from 51 to 100, with chance $1/k$ each. Write $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/n$, with $H_{100} \approx 5.1874$ and $H_{50} \approx 4.4992$.
screens.question: What is the team's chance of success, to four decimal places?

hints.text: Failure has chance $1/51 + \cdots + 1/100$.
That sum is $H_{100} - H_{50}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $H_{100} - H_{50}$ from 1.

byKey.ln2: $1 - \ln 2 \approx 0.3069$ is the limit for many prisoners. At 100 it is still 0.3118.
byKey.fail: That is the chance of failure, $H_{100} - H_{50}$.

explain.text: Failure has chance $1/51 + \cdots + 1/100 = H_{100} - H_{50} \approx 0.6882$. So success is $0.3118$, close to $1 - \ln 2 \approx 0.3069$. Principle: count the one way to fail, then subtract.

screens.title: One prisoner's chance
screens.prose: Edge case. The 100 prisoners follow the numbers, each opening 50.
screens.question: What is prisoner 1's own chance of finding his number?

options.why: That is the team's chance. One prisoner needs only his own cycle short.

options.text: More than $1/2$, thanks to the strategy
options.why: The strategy cannot help one prisoner: his cycle length is equally likely to be 1 to 100.

hints.text: How long is prisoner 1's cycle?
Its length is equally likely to be any of 1 to 100.
Lengths 1 to 50 succeed: $50/100$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how likely his own cycle is to have length at most 50.

byKey.31: 0.31 is the chance that all prisoners succeed.
byKey.more: His cycle length is uniform on 1 to 100, so his chance is exactly $1/2$.
byKey.hundredth: Each opening could find it; 50 openings give $1/2$.

explain.text: The cycle through box 1 has length $k$ with chance $1/100$ for each $k$ from 1 to 100. He succeeds when $k \le 50$, so with chance exactly $1/2$. Only the joint chance changes, from $(1/2)^{100}$ to 0.31.

screens.title: Follow the cycle
screens.prose: Each time, the team failed exactly when one cycle was longer than the openings. With $2m$ prisoners each opening $m$: $$P(\text{win}) = 1 - \sum_{k = m + 1}^{2m} \frac{1}{k} = 1 - (H_{2m} - H_m)$$ The sum is close to the area under $1/x$ from $m$ to $2m$.
screens.question: What does the team's chance approach as the number of prisoners grows?

options.why: That would be true of random opening. Here the failure sum stays near $\ln 2$.
One prisoner's chance is $1/2$. The team's is lower.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sum $1/(m+1) + \cdots + 1/(2m)$ tends to $\int_m^{2m} dx/x$.

byKey.zero: The failure chance tends to $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$, not to 1.
byKey.half: The team's chance is below one prisoner's.

explain.text: $\sum_{k=m+1}^{2m} 1/k$ tends to $\int_m^{2m} dx/x = \ln 2$. So the team's chance falls towards $1 - \ln 2 \approx 0.307$ and never below. Principle: follow the cycle, and the team's fate is one event.

screens.title: Drill: eight prisoners
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Eight prisoners each open 4 of 8 boxes, following the numbers.
screens.question: What is the team's chance of success?

hints.text: Failure is a cycle of length 5, 6, 7 or 8.

byKey.fail: That is the failure chance; subtract it from 1.

explain.text: Failure is a cycle of length 5, 6, 7 or 8, with chance $1/5 + 1/6 + 1/7 + 1/8 = 533/840$. Success is $307/840 \approx 0.3655$, which a count of all 40,320 orders confirms. Principle: one subtraction of a harmonic tail.

screens.title: Drill: read the cycles
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Eight boxes, and each prisoner may open 4. Find the cycles from what each box holds.

state.caption: Box 1 holds 3, box 2 holds 5, box 3 holds 7 and box 4 holds 4. Box 5 holds 8, box 6 holds 2, box 7 holds 1 and box 8 holds 6.

screens.question: Fill in the cycle lengths, then say whether every prisoner succeeds.

hints.text: From box 1: 1 holds 3, 3 holds 7, 7 holds 1.
From box 2: 2, 5, 8, 6, back to 2.
Lengths 3, 4 and 1, all at most 4, so yes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow each chain until it returns to its start.

byKey.r0c1: Box 1 holds 3, box 3 holds 7, box 7 holds 1: three boxes.
byKey.r1c1: Box 2 holds 5, then 8, then 6, then 2: four boxes.
byKey.r3c1: No cycle is longer than 4, so every prisoner finds his number.

explain.text: The cycles are (1, 3, 7), (2, 5, 8, 6) and (4), of lengths 3, 4 and 1. None is longer than 4, so every prisoner succeeds. Principle: the longest cycle decides for everyone.

screens.title: Drill: a long cycle
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Shuffle 100 numbers into 100 boxes at random.
screens.question: What is the chance that some cycle is longer than 50?

hints.text: At most one cycle can exceed 50.
Add $1/k$ for $k$ from 51 to 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chances $1/k$ for $k = 51$ to 100.

byKey.win: That is the chance of no long cycle, when the team wins.
byKey.half: The chances $1/51, \ldots, 1/100$ add to more than a half.

explain.text: Each length $k$ from 51 to 100 has chance $1/k$, and at most one such cycle exists. So the chance is $H_{100} - H_{50} \approx 0.6882$. A long cycle is more likely than not.

screens.title: One swap first
screens.prose: Follow-up. Before anyone enters, one prisoner may look in every box and swap the contents of two boxes. Then the 100 prisoners open 50 each, following the numbers.
screens.question: What is the team's chance now?

options.text: Certain: one swap cuts the only long cycle into two of at most 50
Still about 31%: one swap changes little
options.why: A swap inside a cycle splits it in two. Pick the split, and the long cycle is gone.

options.text: Certain only when the long cycle has even length
options.why: A cycle of 77 splits into 38 and 39. Odd lengths work too.

options.text: About 50%: the swap helps only sometimes
options.why: There is at most one long cycle, and one well-chosen swap always splits it.

hints.text: What does swapping the contents of two boxes in one cycle do?
It splits the cycle into two shorter cycles.
Split a cycle of length $L \le 100$ into $\lfloor L/2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil L/2 \rceil$, both at most 50.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One swap can split the long cycle into two halves.

byKey.same: A swap can split the long cycle into two cycles of at most 50.
byKey.even: Any length up to 100 splits into two parts of at most 50.
byKey.half: There is never more than one long cycle, so one swap always suffices.

explain.text: Swapping the contents of two boxes in one cycle splits it in two. The looker finds the one cycle longer than 50, if any, and splits it into halves of at most 50. Then every cycle is short and everyone succeeds.

ideas: Open your own box, then the box named inside: you find your number exactly when your cycle is short enough.
The team wins exactly when no cycle is longer than the openings, and only one cycle can exceed half.
A cycle of length $k > n/2$ has chance $1/k$, so the chance of success is $1 - (H_n - H_{n/2})$.
summary.trap: Multiplying 100 halves treats the prisoners as independent; the strategy makes them win or lose together.

quiz.prose: Ten prisoners each open 5 of 10 boxes, following the numbers.
quiz.question: What is the team's chance of success?

byKey.fail: That is the failure chance; subtract it from 1.

explain.text: Failure is a cycle of length 6 to 10: $1/6 + 1/7 + 1/8 + 1/9 + 1/10 = 1627/2520$. Success is $893/2520 \approx 0.3544$. The chance falls slowly as the team grows.

quiz.prose: Follow-up. The 100 prisoners may now each open 60 boxes, following the numbers. Take $H_{100} \approx 5.1874$ and $H_{60} \approx 4.6799$.
quiz.question: What is the team's chance of success?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Failure is now a cycle longer than 60.

byKey.fail: That is the failure chance, $H_{100} - H_{60}$.

explain.text: Failure now needs a cycle of length 61 to 100, chance $H_{100} - H_{60} \approx 0.5075$. Success is about 0.4925. Ten more openings each lift the team from 31% to 49%.

quiz.prose: Six numbers lie in six boxes in a random order.
quiz.question: Can the order hold two cycles of length 4?

options.text: Yes, if the boxes are arranged right
options.why: Two cycles of length 4 need 8 boxes, and there are 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the boxes two such cycles would need.

byKey.yes: Cycles share no boxes, so two of length 4 need 8.

explain.text: Cycles never share a box, so two cycles of length 4 need 8 boxes. Six boxes hold at most one cycle longer than 3. That is why the failure chances add.
